title: Hardware timestamps and PTP
text: A latency number needs two things: clocks that agree, and timestamps taken where the packet really is. This is how trading systems get both. We start with the rules, then the hardware, then the protocol.

title: Why it matters
text: Regulators set a bar. Under the EU's clock rules, a firm using high frequency trading must stay within 100 microseconds of UTC, and timestamp to 1 microsecond or better. And any one-way latency you measure between two machines is only as good as the clocks at each end.

title: Where to stamp
text: A software timestamp is taken when the packet enters the kernel, after the interrupt and the driver have run. A hardware timestamp is taken by the network card itself, as the frame arrives. On Linux, the SO_TIMESTAMPING socket option asks for either. The hardware value comes back in a control message, and transmit stamps return through the socket's error queue.

title: The PTP exchange
text: The Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588, steers a clock to a master over the network. The master sends Sync at t1, and the slave receives it at t2. The slave sends a Delay Request at t3. The master receives it at t4, and sends that time back in a Delay Response. Now the slave holds four timestamps, and two equations.

title: Worked example
text: Say Sync leaves at 1,000 nanoseconds and arrives at 1,650, by the slave's clock. The Delay Request leaves at 2,000 and arrives at 2,250. The offset is 650 minus 250, over 2: the slave runs 200 nanoseconds ahead. The path delay is 650 plus 250, over 2, which is 450 nanoseconds.

title: The catch: symmetry
text: That math assumes both directions take the same time. Any asymmetry turns into offset error, at half its size. Queues in switches are the usual culprit. So PTP-aware switches act as boundary clocks, which run a clock of their own, or as transparent clocks, which correct for the time each message spent inside them. So if one direction takes 100 nanoseconds longer than the other, the clock ends up 50 nanoseconds off.

title: In the lab
text: On Linux, ptp4l runs the protocol with hardware timestamps by default, and phc2sys keeps the system clock in step with the card. The lab's hot threads stamp with raw rdtsc ticks: a few nanoseconds, no system call. They are converted to nanoseconds off the hot path, with a ratio calibrated against the monotonic clock at startup.

title: Takeaway
text: Stamp in hardware, synchronise with PTP, and keep the paths symmetric. Otherwise your latency numbers are measuring your clocks.
